extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, agents, attorneys, and CNIPA examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and prosecuting patent applications before China's CNIPA (2026 Guidelines), including subject-matter eligibility, inventiveness assessment, utility models, AI/big-data-specific disclosure and examination issues, and procedural restrictions such as dual filing and invalidation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and Big Data — legality and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment addresses the legality and ethics of AI and Big Data applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and applicants should consider legal and ethical issues when evaluating AI/big-data-related inventions; the Guidelines explicitly bring legality and ethics into the examination considerations for such applications. (Page notes the topic areas covered but does not list specific ethical/legal tests on this extract.)

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and Big Data — sufficient disclosure for algorithm/data inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient disclosure requirements for algorithm/data-related inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm- and data-related inventions must meet disclosure requirements (enablement/written description) appropriate to the technology — e.g., sufficient detail about algorithms, models, data, training processes, parameters, or workflows so a skilled person can implement the claimed solution. The 2026 revision explicitly emphasizes disclosure sufficiency for AI/data inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and Big Data — inventiveness assessment for AI/ML inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventiveness assessment of AI/ML inventions is addressed in the Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA provides guidance on how to assess inventive step (non-obviousness) for AI/ML inventions, recognizing technology-specific considerations. The Guidelines aim to clarify how inventiveness should be judged for AI/ML technical solutions (details are in the full text beyond this summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness assessment applies to the claimed technical solution as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed technical solution should be subject to the inventiveness assessment test in its entirety, rather than a test of inventiveness of certain technical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing inventive step, examiners must evaluate the claimed invention as an integrated technical solution — avoid isolating or dissecting only particular features for inventiveness. This principle affects claim drafting and how prior art is compared to the claim in its whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual filing restriction (invention patent vs utility model)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant files an invention patent application and a parallel utility model application on the same day with mutual cross references ('Dual Filing'), the applicant must, upon receiving a notice of allowance for the invention patent, abandon the parallel utility model application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants engaging in dual filing should expect to forgo the utility model if the corresponding invention patent is allowed; prosecutorial strategy must account for this mandatory abandonment upon allowance of the invention patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith requirement for invalidation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for invalidation will not be accepted if it is not based on true intention of the petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines reinforce good faith principles (referencing Article 20 of Chinese Patent Law). Parties seeking invalidation must demonstrate genuine intent; sham or abusive invalidation petitions can be rejected. This affects both third-party invalidation practice and post-grant dispute behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step test for inventiveness (problem–solution approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: CNIPA uses a three-step approach similar to the EPO's problem–solution method to assess inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three steps are: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine the distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Examiners should follow these sequential steps when evaluating inventive step; the approach emphasizes identification of the actual technical problem and distinguishing features rather than hindsight reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter exclusions (Article 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories are excluded from patentability under Article 25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed non-patentable subject matter includes: scientific discoveries; rules and methods for mental activities; methods for diagnosis and treatment of diseases; animal and plant varieties; substances obtained by means of nuclear transformation; and designs that are mainly used for marking patterns/colors/combinations on plane prints. Applicants should frame claims to avoid falling squarely within these excluded categories or show technical character where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model scope and inventiveness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models cover product shape, structure, or combinations and (post-2024 amendments) are subject to inventiveness examination with a lower bar than invention patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility model protection is distinct from invention patents and applies to structural/shape aspects of products. While utility models now undergo inventiveness examination, the threshold is lower than for invention patents — practitioners should consider strategic filing choices (utility model vs invention patent) and draft claims consistent with the scope and inventiveness expectations for utility models in China.
